problem_data.story:
THE RETURNED ONE
By HERBERT D. KASTLE
Adapted for Dravonian Setting

There was the usual welcoming crowd for a celebrity, and the usual speeches by the usual politicians who met her at the transit station which had once been twenty miles outside of Copperfield, but which the growing city had since engulfed and placed well within its boundaries. But everything wasn't usual. The crowd was quiet, and the mayor didn't seem quite as at-ease as he'd been on his last big welcoming—for Dr. Manuel Fuller, one of the team that had successfully mapped the consciousness patterns of deep-space travelers. His Honor's handclasp was somewhat moist and cold. His Honor's eyes held a trace of remoteness.

Still, she was the honored home-comer, the successful returnee, the hometown woman who had made good in a big way, and they took the triumphal tour up Central Avenue to the new plaza and the grandstand. There she sat between the mayor and a nervous young student chosen as homecoming representative, and looked out at the municipal bands, the Regional Guard, the youth organizations and civic groups. Several of the philosophical societies in town had shown indecision as to how to instruct their members to treat her. But they had all come around. The tremendous national interest, the fact that she was the First Returned, had made them come around. It was obvious by now that they would have to adjust as they'd adjusted to all the other firsts taking place in these—as the media outlets had dubbed the start of the new era—the Age of Restoration.

She was glad when the official greeting was over. Patricia Alvarez was a very tired woman and she had come farther, traveled longer through darker territory, than any person who'd ever lived before. She wanted a meal at her own table, a kiss from her husband, a word from her daughter, and later to see some old friends and a relative or two. She didn't want to talk about the journey. She wanted to forget the immediacy, the urgency, the terror; then perhaps she would talk.

Or would she? For she had very little to tell. She had traveled and she had returned and her voyage was very much like the voyages of the great explorers, from the ancient archaeologists who first opened the tombs onward—long, dull periods of time passing, passing, and then the arrival.

The house had changed. She saw that as soon as the official vehicle let her off at 45 Meridian Street. The change was, she knew, for the better. They had put a garden in front. They had rehabilitated, spruced up, almost rebuilt the entire outside and grounds. But she was sorry. She had wanted it to be as before.

The head of the Citizens' Council and the chief administrator, who had escorted her on this trip from the plaza, didn't ask to go in with her. She was glad. She'd had enough of strangers. Not that she was through with strangers. There were dozens of them up and down the street, standing beside parked vehicles, looking at her. But when she looked back at them, their eyes dropped, they turned away, they began moving off. She was still too much the First Returned to have her gaze met.

She walked up what had once been a simple path and was now an ornate stone walkway. She climbed the new steps and raised the electronic chime, hearing the soft tone sound within. She was surprised that she'd had to do this. She'd thought Tomás would be watching at a window.

And perhaps he had been watching... but he hadn't opened the door.

The door opened; she looked at him. It hadn't been too long and he hadn't changed at all. He was still the tall, gentle man she'd loved in university, the tall, gentle man she'd married fourteen years ago. Eva was with him. They held onto each other as if seeking mutual support, the thirty-five-year-old man and twelve-year-old girl. They looked at her, and then both moved forward, still together. She said, "It's good to be home!"

Tomás nodded and, still holding to Eva with one hand, put the other arm around her. She kissed him—his neck, his cheek—and all the old jokes came to mind, the jokes of travel-weary, research-weary scientists, the and-then-I'll-put-my-pack-aside jokes that spoke of terrible hunger. He was trembling, and even as his lips came up to touch hers she felt the difference, and because of this difference she turned with urgency to Eva and picked her up and hugged her and said, because she could think of nothing else to say, "What a big girl, what a big girl."

Eva stood in her arms as if her feet were still planted on the floor, and she didn't look at her mother but somewhere beyond her. "I didn't grow much while you were gone, Mom. Dad says I don't eat enough."

So she put her down and told herself that it would all change, that everything would loosen up just as her supervisor, Director Stephen Gupta, had said it would early this morning before she left the capital in Rosewood Province.

"Give it some time," Gupta had said. "You need the time; they need the time. And for the love of reason, don't be sensitive."

Tomás was leading her into the living room, his hand lying still in hers, a cool, dead bird lying still in hers. She sat down on the couch, he sat down beside her—but he had hesitated. She wasn't being sensitive; he had hesitated. Her husband had hesitated before sitting down beside her.

Gupta had said her position was analogous to the ancient archaeologists who'd first returned from sealed tombs, to the early consciousness studies researchers who'd mapped the boundaries of death—but more so. Gupta had said lots of things, but even Gupta who had worked with her all the way, who had engineered the entire fantastic journey using cutting-edge biotechnology—even Gupta the prize winner, the multi-degreed genius in administration, had not actually spoken to her as one person to another.

The eyes. It always showed in their eyes.

She looked across the room at Eva, standing in the doorway, a girl already tall, already showing the features of young adulthood. It was like looking into the mirror and seeing herself twenty-three years ago. But Eva's face was drawn, was worried in a way that few twelve-year-old faces are.

"How's it going with your media production classes?" she asked.

"Mom, it's the second month of summer break."

"Well, then, before summer break?"

"Pretty good."

Tomás said, "She made top marks the six-month period before break, and she made top marks the six-month period you went away, Patricia."

She nodded, remembering that, remembering everything, remembering the warmth of their farewell, the warmth of Eva's farewell, their tears as she left for the experimental facility in Ashford Province. They had feared for her, having read of the many procedures gone wrong even in the most controlled experimental design.

They had been right to worry. She had suffered much after that incident. But now they should be rejoicing, because she had made it through the long process. Eva suddenly said, "I got to go, Mom. I promised Akira and the others I'd help with the documentary project. It's Inter-Regional Youth Media, you know. I got to keep my word." Without waiting for an answer, she waved her hand—it shook; a twelve-year-old girl's hand that shook—and ran from the room and from the house.

She and Tomás sat beside each other, and she wanted badly to take him in her arms, and yet she didn't want to oppress him. She stood up. "I'm very tired. I'd like to lie down a while." Which wasn't true, because she'd been lying down all the months of the way back.

He said, "Of course. How foolish of me, expecting you to sit around and make small talk and pick up just where you left off."

She nodded. But that was exactly what she wanted to do—make small talk and pick up just where she'd left off. But they didn't expect it of her; they wouldn't let her; they felt she had changed too much.

He led her upstairs and along the corridor past Eva's room and past the small guest room to their bedroom. This, too, had changed. It was newly painted and it had new furniture. She saw twin beds separated by an ornate little table with an ornate little lamp, and this looked more ominous a barrier to her than the twelve-foot security fence around the experimental facility.

"Which one is mine," she asked, and tried to smile.

He also tried to smile. "The one near the window. You always liked the fresh air, the morning light. You always said it helped you to organize your thoughts when you were working at the research center. You always said it reminded you—being able to see the sky—that you were going to complete your work, and that you were going to return to this bed again."

"Not this bed," she murmured, and was a little sorry afterward.

"No, not this bed," he said quickly. "Your professional society donated the bedroom set and I really didn't know—" He waved his hand, his face pale.

She was sure then that he had known, and that the beds and the barrier between them were his own choice, if only an unconscious choice. She went to the bed near the window, stripped off her formal jacket, began to take off her shirt, but then remembered that some scars still showed. She waited for him to leave the room.

He said, "Well then, rest up, dear," and went out.

She took off her shirt and saw herself in the mirror on the opposite wall; and then took off her undershirt. The body scars were faint, the scars running in long lines, one crossing her chest, the other slicing diagonally across her upper abdomen to disappear under her trousers. There were several more on her back, and one on her right thigh. They'd been treated properly with advanced biotechnology and would soon disappear. But he had never seen them.

Perhaps he never would. Perhaps careful clothing and dark rooms would keep them from him until they were gone.

Which was not what she'd considered at all important on leaving Regional Medical early this morning; which was something she found distasteful, something she felt beneath them both. And, at the same time, she began to understand that there would be many things, previously beneath them both, which would have to be considered. He had changed; Eva had changed; all the people she knew had probably changed—because they thought she had changed.

She was tired of thinking. She lay down and closed her eyes. She let herself taste bitterness, unhappiness, a loneliness she had never known before.

But sometime later, as she was dozing off, a sense of reassurance began filtering into her mind. After all, she was still Patricia Alvarez, the same person who had left home thirteen months ago, with a love for family and friends which was, if anything, stronger than before. Once she could communicate this, the strangeness would disappear and the First Returned would again become good old Patricia. It was little enough to ask for—a return to old values, old relationships, the normalcies of the everyday instead of the chaos of the spotlight. It would certainly be granted to her.

She slept.

Dinner was at seven p.m. Her mother came; her Uncle Leo and Aunt Marcus came. Together with Tomás, Eva and herself, they made six, and ate in the dining room at the big table.

Before she'd become the First Returned, it would have been a noisy affair. Her family had never been noted for a lack of energy, a lack of conversation, and Eva had always chosen mealtimes—especially with company present—to describe everything and anything that had happened to her during the day. And Tomás himself had always chatted, especially with her mother, though they didn't agree about political philosophy. Still, it had been good-natured; the general tone of their lives had been good-natured.

This wasn't good-natured. Exactly what it was she wasn't sure. "Stiff" was perhaps the word.

They began with soup, Tomás and Mother serving quickly, efficiently from the kitchen, then sitting down at the table. She looked at Mother as she raised her first spoonful of warm broth, and said, "Looking well as always." It was nothing new; she'd said it many many times before, but her mother had always reacted with a bright smile and a quip something like, "Well enough for my age, you mean." This time she burst into tears. It shocked her. But what shocked her even more was the fact that no one looked up, commented, made any attempt to comfort her; no one indicated in any way that a woman was sobbing at the table.

She was sitting directly across from Mother, and reached out and touched her left hand which lay limply beside the silverware. She didn't move it—she hadn't touched her once beyond that first, quick, strangely-cool embrace at the door—then a few seconds later she withdrew it and let it drop out of sight.

So there she was, Patricia Alvarez, at home with the family. So there she was, the pioneer returned, waiting to be treated as a human being.

The soup bowls were cleared away and the main course served. Uncle Leo began to talk. "The most fascinating organizational behavior study you ever did see," he boomed in his powerful professor's voice. "Still ongoing. We'll publish before—" At that point he looked at Patricia, and Patricia nodded encouragement, desperately interested in this normalcy, and Leo's voice died away. He looked down at his plate, mumbled, "Food's getting cold," and began to eat. His hand shook a little; his weathered face was not quite as confident as Patricia remembered it.

Aunt Marcus made a few quavering statements about the Regional Arts Council, and Patricia looked across the table to where she sat between Leo and Mother—her husband and daughter bracketed her, and yet she felt alone—and said, "I've missed working on my time management projects. Here it is late summer and I haven't organized a single schedule."

Aunt Marcus smiled, if you could call it that—a pitiful twitching of the lips—and nodded. She threw her eyes in Patricia's direction, and past her, and then down to her plate. Mother, who was still sniffling, said, "I have a terrible headache. I'm going to lie down in the guest room a while." She touched Patricia's shoulder in passing—her affectionate, effusive mother who would embrace stray animals and strange children, who had often overwhelmed her with an excess of physical and verbal affection—she barely touched Patricia's shoulder and fled.

So now five of them sat at the table. The meat was served—thin, rare slices of protein, the juices running warmly from the center. She cut into it and raised a forkful to her mouth, then glanced at Eva and said, "Looks fresh enough to have been prepared this morning." Eva said, "Yeah, Mom." Aunt Marcus put down her knife and fork and murmured something to her husband. Leo cleared his throat and said Marcus was developing new dietary preferences and he guessed she was going into the living room for a while. "She'll be back for dessert, of course," he said, his laugh sounding forced.

Patricia looked at Tomás; Tomás was busy with his plate. Patricia looked at Eva; Eva was busy with her plate. Patricia looked at Leo; Leo was chewing, gazing out over their heads to the kitchen. Patricia looked at Marcus; she was disappearing into the living room.

She brought her fist down on the table. The settings jumped; a glass overturned, spilling water. She brought it down again and again. They were all standing now. She sat there and pounded the table with her right fist—Patricia Alvarez, who would never have thought of making such a scene before, but who was now so sick and tired of being treated as the First Returned, of being stood back from, looked at in awe of, felt in fear of, that she could have smashed more than a table.

Tomás said, "Patricia!"

She said, voice hoarse, "Shut up. Go away. Let me eat alone. I'm sick of the lot of you."

Mother and Leo returned a few minutes later where she sat forcing food down her throat. Mother said, "Patricia dear—" She didn't answer. She began to cry, and Patricia was glad she left the house then. She had never said anything really harsh to her mother. She was afraid this would have been the time. Leo merely cleared his throat and mumbled something about getting together again soon and "come visit the research center" and he, too, was gone. Marcus never did manage to speak to her.

She finished her meal and waited. Soon Tomás came in with the special dessert he'd been preparing half the day—a magnificent layered cake. He served her, and cut portions for himself and Eva. He hesitated near her chair, and when she made no comment he called the girl. Then the three of them were sitting, facing the empty side of the table. They ate the cake. Eva finished first and got up and said, "Hey, I promised—"

"You promised your friends you'd work on media production or study information theory or something; anything to get away from your mother."

Eva's head dropped and she muttered, "No, Mom."

Tomás said, "She'll stay home, Patricia. We'll spend an evening together—talking, watching programs, playing games."

Eva said, "Sure, Mom, if you want to."

Patricia stood up. "The question is not whether I want to. You both know I want to. The question is whether you want to."

They answered together that of course they wanted to. But their eyes—her husband's and daughter's eyes—could not meet hers, and so she said she was going to her room because she was, after all, very tired and would in all probability continue to be very tired for a long, long time and that they shouldn't count on her for normal social interaction.

She fell asleep quickly, lying there in her clothes.

But she didn't sleep long. Tomás shook her and she opened her eyes to a lighted room. "Akira and Manuel are here." She blinked at him. He smiled, and it seemed his old smile. "They're so anxious to see you, Patricia. I could barely keep Akira from coming up and waking you herself. They want to go out and see the city. Please, Patricia, say you will."

She sat up. "Akira," she muttered. "Akira and Manuel." They'd had wonderful times together, from university on. Akira and Manuel, their oldest and closest friends. Perhaps this would begin her real homecoming.

See the city? They'd celebrate it properly!

It didn't turn out that way. She was disappointed; but then again, she'd also expected it. This entire first day at home had conditioned her to expect nothing good. They went to the entertainment complex, and Akira sounded very much the way she always had—quick-witted and full of laughter and full of stories. She hugged Tomás the way she always had, and embraced Patricia warmly (but not the way she always had—so much more carefully, almost remotely), and insisted they all drink more than was good for them as she always had. And for once, Patricia was ready to go along on the drinking. For once, she matched Akira glass for glass.

They didn't stay at the entertainment complex very long. At ten o'clock they crossed the plaza to Meridian's Café, where Akira and the others ordered food and coffee and Patricia went right on drinking. Tomás said something to her, but she merely smiled and waved her hand and gulped another ounce of oblivion.

There was music and dancing in Meridian's Café. She'd been there many times before, and she was sure several of the patrons recognized her. But except for a few abortive glances in her direction, it was as if she were a stranger in a city halfway around the world.

At midnight, she was still drinking. The others wanted to leave, but she said, "I haven't danced with my friend Manuel." Her tongue was thick, her mind was blurred, and yet she could read the strange expression on his face—friendly Manuel, who'd always joked with her, who'd made a ritual of joking with her. Friendly Manuel, who now looked as if he were going to be sick.

"So let's dance," she said and stood up.

They were on the dance floor. She held him close, and hummed and chatted. And through the alcoholic haze saw he was a stiff-smiled, stiff-bodied, mechanical dancing partner.

The music finished; they walked back to the booth. Akira said, "Time to head home."

Patricia said, "First one dance with my loving husband."

She and Tomás danced. She didn't hold him close as she had Manuel. She waited for him to come close on his own, and he did, and yet he didn't. Because while he put himself against her, there was something in his face—no, in his eyes; it always showed in the eyes—that made her know he was trying to be the old Tomás and not succeeding. This time when the music ended, she was ready to go home.

They rode back through Pearlbrook District, she and Tomás in the rear of Akira's vehicle, Manuel driving because Akira had drunk just a little too much, Akira singing and telling an occasional story, and somehow not her old self. No one was their old self. No one would ever be their old self with the First Returned.

They turned left, to take the short cut along Memorial Road, and Akira finished a story about a consciousness researcher and a media personality and looked at her husband and then past him at the long, ornate fence paralleling the road. "Hey," she said, pointing, "do you know what they say about that place?"

Manuel glanced to the left, and so did Patricia and Tomás. Manuel made a little sound, and Tomás seemed to stop breathing, but Akira went on a while longer, not yet aware of her supposed faux pas.

"You know what they say?" she repeated, turning to the back seat, the laughter bubbling up. "You know what, folks?"

Manuel said, "Did you notice the new construction near—"

Patricia said, "No, Akira, what do they say?"

Akira said, "They say it's—" And then she caught herself and waved her hand and muttered, "I forgot what I was going to say."

"They say it's where people go to rest forever," Patricia said, and looked through the window, past the ornate fence, into the large memorial park at the fleeting monuments. She remembered her own certificate, the one Gupta had shown her—dated nine months ago next Tuesday, signed by the attending physician, filed with the provincial registry. "Cause: catastrophic trauma sustained during laboratory incident." She had read it three times before believing it referred to her.

The vehicle was filled with horrified silence when there should have been nothing but laughter, or irritation at a too-old observation. "Maybe you should let me out right here," Patricia said. "I'm home—or that's what everyone seems to think. Maybe I should lie down in one of those crypts. Maybe that would satisfy people. Maybe that's the only way to act, like something from ancient metaphysics or horror stories."

Tomás said, "Oh, Patricia, don't, don't!"

The vehicle raced along the road, crossed a main thoroughfare, went four blocks and pulled to a stop. She didn't bother saying good night. She didn't wait for Tomás. She just got out and walked up the stone path and entered the house.

"Patricia," Tomás whispered from the guest room doorway, "I'm so sorry—"

"There's nothing to be sorry about. It's just a matter of time. It'll all work out in time."

"Yes," he said quickly, "that's it. I need a little time. We all need a little time. Because it's so strange, Patricia. Because it's so frightening. I should have told you that the moment you walked in. I think I've hurt you terribly, we've all hurt you terribly, by trying to hide that we're frightened."

"I'm going to stay in the guest room," she said, "for as long as necessary. For good if need be."

"How could it be for good? How, Patricia?"

That question was perhaps the first firm basis for hope she'd had since returning. And there was something else; what Gupta had told her, even as Gupta himself had reacted as all people did.

"There are others in the facility, Tomás. Eight that I know of in the suspension chambers right now, going through the same process I did. My colleague, Dr. Nelson, who was injured in the same incident—she's going to be next. Her damage was more extensive, so it's taking longer, but she's almost ready. And there'll be many more, Tomás. The government is going to use this technology whenever they possibly can from now on. When a young and healthy person suffers catastrophic trauma—when their body can still be recovered—they'll go into the chambers. They'll begin the protocol. So people have to get used to us. And the old stories, the old terrors, the ugly old superstitions have to fade, because in time each place will have some of us; because in time it'll be an ordinary thing."

Tomás said, "Yes, and I'm so grateful that you're here, Patricia. Please believe that. Please be patient with me and Eva and—" He paused. "There's one question."

She knew what the question was. It had been the first asked her by everyone from the Premier of Dravonia on down, a question that touched on consciousness studies and the nature of existence itself.

"I experienced nothing," she said. "It was as if I slept those eight and a half months—slept without dreaming. The monitors showed no brain activity during the suspension phase, and I have no memories from that time. No metaphysical revelations, no journey through consciousness. Just... absence. Whatever I was before the incident, I simply wasn't, and then I was again."

He came to her and touched her face with his lips, and she was satisfied.

Later, half asleep, she heard a dog howling, and remembered stories of how they announced death and the presence of things that should have stayed buried. She shivered and pulled the covers closer to her and luxuriated in being safe in her own home.

THE END
